short_definition: A bull market is a sustained period of generally rising asset prices, while a bear market is a sustained decline, often informally defined as a fall of 20% or more from a recent peak.
explanation: 'Bull' and 'bear' describe the overall direction and mood of a market over months or years, not single-day moves. The 20% threshold for a bear market is a media and industry convention, not an official rule. A smaller drop, often around 10%, is usually called a correction. Both labels only become clear in hindsight.

These terms matter because they help you set realistic expectations. Declines have happened repeatedly in stock market history, and how investors react to them can affect long-term results more than the decline itself. Past recoveries do not guarantee future ones, though, and some markets have taken many years to get back to earlier peaks.

The main risk is trying to time the switch between bull and bear markets. Calling turning points reliably is very hard, and investors who sell after a fall can miss part of any rebound. Whether to change your plan during a downturn depends on your time horizon, your risk tolerance and when you need the cash. For personal decisions, a licensed adviser can help.
example: Illustrative example: An index rises from 1,000 to 1,600 over several years, which is a bull market. It then falls to 1,200. The drop is (1,600 − 1,200) ÷ 1,600 = 25%, which most people would call a bear market. A $10,000 portfolio that tracked the index exactly would be worth about $7,500 at the low.
common_mistake: Treating the 'bear market' headline as a signal to sell everything and wait for an all-clear. Recoveries are usually only obvious after they have already started.
title: Bull Market vs Bear Market
